manual.p: The return value 0 from a method may show that there was some error, but not what the problem was. It is common to combine return values of this kind with a way to find out the nature of the problem. This can be done with special error codes, that your program can retrieve from somewhere. Lets look at this example, which opens a file on disk for reading:

item.p: Stdio.File is a stream that can be used to read from a file on fisk. It is similar to the data type FILE in C, and the classes ifstream and ofstream in C++.
!localfile->open(file_name, "r") means exactly the same thing as localfile->open(file_name, "r") == 0.
It is common to use the logical not operator (!) to check if something is 0.
errno is a method in the class Stdio.File, and can be used io check what kind of error has occurred in a particular stream. It returns an error code. errno is not a global variable, as in C.
strerror returns a string that describes the error number given as an argument.

manual.p: If the file couldn't be opened, the program's output will look something like this:
manual.out: Couldn't open 'foobar.txt'. No such file or directory (errno = 2).
